A language switch keeps both the result and the note; a new run removes the note, and so does anything that replaces or drops the result (the Zone File's own Run on its Live tab, a new import, Forget), while a Run again that brings nothing new (a CT lookup that finds nothing) leaves it. The Zone File's note reads "Live check from 14:02", so it says what it is about on every tab. IP Intel matches kept rows against the servers as they are on return. A result over the memory bound comes back as its query, filled in, with "The result from <time> was too large to keep" and Run again; one whose query no link carries (IP Intel over 40 entries) opens empty, with the same note and no Run again. The oldest result goes first; a result only looked at again keeps its age. "Delete all local data" forgets the target, the kept results and what the tools with module state hold (Subdomains' and SSL Targets' box and last scan, Bulk Resolve's list and last job — running ones are stopped — the Certificate view's "No file?" field and per-certificate CAA / CT / DANE results, the zone), and the tool on screen opens again, bare; a reload or closing the tab forgets the page session too.

**Copy summary (`ui/summary-button.js` over §5.32).** A finished result has **Copy summary** (Markdown for a Jira ticket or a Slack thread) and a small **Plain text** button next to it (the same lines without Markdown) in its result header: Domain Health's hero next to "Report (JSON)", the Subdomains run's header (above the tabs, so every tab has it), SSL Targets' results head, Global DNS's links row, Zone File's summary bar, the Certificate overview's actions, Renewal readiness's summary card, DNS Lookup's summary card, above IP Intel's stat cards and in the DMARC & TLS reports' results head. They are disabled while a run is going (Domain Health's too, while a new check runs over the previous report; a cancelled Subdomains scan copies what it found; SSL Targets waits for a finished scan) and read the view's facts at click time, in the UI language. `SummaryButton({ kind, facts, url, inventory: false | 'names' | 'count', disabled })` returns `{ el, setDisabled, text(format) }`; `url` is the permalink of the result the facts describe (Domain Health: the report's domain and the DKIM selectors it was checked with). The copy reuses `CopyButton` (the "Copied" feedback, a toast naming the format: `toastOnCopy` takes a text) with its `onFail` option: a browser that refuses the clipboard gets the text in a dialog, selected, to copy by hand (Ctrl+C / ⌘C, or touch and hold on a phone). The tooltip says what a summary holds — only what the page shows and a link to the page (Zone File, Certificate and DMARC & TLS reports: without the files' contents); nothing from the server list, except SSL Targets (`'names'`: the servers that need the certificate, as its Servers tab shows them) and IP Intel (`'count'`: how many addresses are in the list, never a name). `resultPermalink(root)` gives the link of the first shown summary that has a result, for the print header.

**Print.** The dark palette is screen-only (`@media screen` around the dark tokens), so printing from dark mode gives dark text on white paper. The print stylesheet (style.css, plus a block per view for its own form) hides the header, nav, footer, page header, toasts, dialogs, progress bars, every button and form field, segmented controls, file drops, table toolbars / expanders and the tabs that are not selected; it prints scrollers whole, repeats table headers with their labels (a sortable header's `.dt-sort` button is `display: contents` on paper: Chrome leaves buttons out of a repeated header row), keeps rows, alerts, stat cards and key-value rows from breaking across pages, wraps code and tightens tables. What is drawn with backgrounds keeps them on paper (`print-color-adjust: exact`: Domain Health's traffic light, the Certificate overview's lifetime bar). A cell breaks only between words (`overflow-wrap: break-word`, never `anywhere`, which lets a column shrink to one character); addresses and host names stay whole (`nowrap` in the view blocks: SSL Targets' address columns `scan-col-ips`, IP Intel's address, Global DNS's addresses and names, Subdomains' and Domain Health's names and addresses), and IP Intel's operator and network cells drop their screen minimum widths so its table fits the page. On `beforeprint` app.js opens every closed `<details>` of the page (a Disclosure's content belongs on paper) and puts a `.print-head` on top — the app, the page title, "Printed <UTC time>" and the permalink as a link: the one of the result on paper (`resultPermalink`, the link its Copy summary carries), else the route with the view's own shareable params (§5.32 `permalinkParams`); never inventory data or file contents. `afterprint` closes what it opened and removes the header. `Page.printToPDF` fires both events.

**Globalping gate (`ui/globalping-gate.js`).** Every Globalping send of the app goes through it. Consent is kept per purpose (`'verify'`, `'mta-sts'`, `'renew-http01'`, `'ns-parity'`, `'origin-compare'`, `'takeover-http'` — Subdomains › Takeover risks' page check, one HTTP GET of `http://<host>/` per host whose service's page decides, ten at most, asked again above three probes, `'isp-dns'` — Global DNS › ISP resolvers, a batch above 20 probes asks again) for the page session only — each feature sends different data, so each shows its own privacy text once — and is never stored; "Delete all local data" clears it and the shared quota. `sharedQuota()` / `noteQuota(q)` keep the latest reading for every view (the anonymous quota is per IP address), `liveQuota(q)` drops a reading whose window has passed, `whenText(resetAt)` words a reset ("in 42 minutes", never "… ago"), `measurementUrl(id)` is the only public measurement link. `gateProbes(ctx, { purpose, probes, privacy, signal, confirm })` is the flow of a one-click feature: the shared client (`ctx.getGlobalping`), one free `/limits` read (a failed read falls back to the last reading of the open window, else the anonymous limit, and the dialog says so), `{ status: 'quota', resetAt }` without asking when the quota cannot cover the probes, the consent + cost dialog (`confirmProbes`) on the purpose's first send, then `{ status: 'go', client, quota }` — the caller sends. SSL Targets › Verify keeps its batch flow on the same consent and quota.

**Long jobs outside their view (`ui/jobs.js` over §5.38).** A Subdomains or SSL Targets scan, a Bulk Resolve run and a Domain portfolio check register a job when they start (`startJob({ view })`, updated from the scanner's stage / progress hooks with `scanFraction`, or from the bulk job's row events with `bulkFraction`; the portfolio's: the share of its domains done) and end it on done / cancel / error. While jobs run: the tab title reads "(62%) <page> · DomainScope" ("(%62)" in Turkish; the least advanced job; the shell sets the page's own title through `setBaseTitle`), the running view's navigation entry carries a progress ring (replacing the busy dot; screen-reader text "running, 62% done") also while another view is open, and the favicon's href is a badged SVG `data:` URL (CSP `img-src data:`), restored when the last job ends. Renders are throttled by timers, not animation frames, so a background tab still updates. Once a job has run 30 s, its panel offers **Notify me when done** (bell): the permission is asked only on that click, the opt-in lasts for the page session (never stored; "Delete all local data" drops it; pressed again it turns off; a toggle whose label stays the same — `aria-pressed` and a pressed look say it is on), a blocked permission is said instead (a refusal on the click moves the keyboard focus to that sentence; while the browser's prompt is open the button is busy — `aria-busy`, `aria-disabled`, a spinner — but never disabled, so the focus stays on it for any other answer), and a desktop notification ("Bulk Resolve finished" + the done-toast text; a failure too, never a cancel) is sent when a job over 30 s ends while its view is not in a visible, focused tab; a click on it focuses the tab and opens the view. Never offered where the page cannot show a notification itself (`pageNotifications`: Chromium on Android — a tablet too, `userAgentData.platform` — has the permission prompt but only a service worker may notify, and the page does not notify through one); a browser whose constructor still throws turns the opt-in off for the page session and says so in a toast. With `prefers-reduced-motion` the ring does not animate and the favicon moves in 10 % steps.

**Workspaces (app.js, `ui/workspace-ui.js`, `ui/workspace-panel.js` over §5.39–§5.42).** The header shows the active workspace after the current-target chip (`data-control="workspace"`: a briefcase, the name cut with an ellipsis, "Default" / "Varsayılan" for Default); below 720 px it sits at the top of the Tools menu instead (`data-control="workspace-menu"`). Either opens the **Workspaces** dialog (its module and `assets/css/workspace.css` load on first use; a failure offers the reload of a stale page like any lazy module): the list (Default first; the active one marked; Switch, Rename inline, Delete with a confirmation — never Default; deleting the active one switches to Default first), a new workspace (created and switched to; empty and taken names — Default's name in either language included — refused in place); the current workspace's **recent domains** (a click makes one the current target, filled in everywhere, and closes the dialog; Clear the list), **expected CAs** (one per line, each shown as a known CA or as text) and **notes**, both saved as typed (400 ms) into the workspace they were typed in, flushed before a switch or when the dialog closes; the **accepted risks** (§5.95: their counts — active, ending within 14 days, expired —, one line each with its kind, domain, ref, end date, owner and reason and a Remove, **Remove the expired ones**, **Export waivers.json** — the runner's `--waivers` input — and **Import waivers.json**, merged: an entry for the same item replaces the one there, the entries that cannot be read are said and left out); and the **hand-over file**: Export with an optional password (twice; ≥ 8 characters; both fields emptied afterwards) downloads `domainscope-workspace-<name>-<stamp>.json`, or with a password `domainscope-workspace-encrypted-<stamp>.json` (no name), and says whether it is encrypted (a password of spaces only is refused); Import (a .json read in the browser) asks for the password of a sealed file (a wrong one or a changed file: "Wrong password, or the file was changed after it was exported. Nothing was imported."), then shows what it holds (with its origin map's entries, and "remembering origins is on" when the file switches that on in the workspace it opens as) and offers **Import as a new workspace** (a free name, switched to) and, when a workspace of that name exists (Default for a file exported from Default), **Replace "<name>"** after a confirmation. A **switch** asks first when something runs that it would stop (`ui/jobs.js runningWork`: the long jobs, and what `registerRunning` adds — a Reverse DNS sweep, a Renewal readiness HTTP-01 test, Retire an IP's check, and on Globalping a Verify batch, a comparison with new name servers (`par.switchRunning`) or of an old and a new server (`oc.switchRunning`), whose probes stay used; "Still running here: … Switching to "<name>" stops the work in progress") or when the server list has changes that are not saved (a view's optional `unsaved()` export — the Servers view has one — or its draft kept in `state.session.inventoryDraft`), then forgets the page session and makes the new workspace's most recent domain the current target, and opens the tool on screen again with it filled in (`carryRoute`); every target a tool runs on goes to the top of the active workspace's recent list. The boot waits for `state.ready`; storage unavailable (no localStorage or a memory-only workspace store) is said once in a toast. **Delete all local data** (Settings, About; `deleteAllLocalData`) deletes every workspace with the IndexedDB database and says so ("every workspace (its IndexedDB database too)", also for a database the page could not open and worked around in memory; without IndexedDB, that the workspaces were only in this tab; with storage blocked altogether, that nothing had been saved: `clearedMessage`), or why not all of it could go, in words (`storageErrorText`: a full storage, a refusal, a database another tab kept open or that did not open in time, a workspace deleted in another tab; another error quoted). A write that failed says the same reason ("Not saved: …"), never as a success: a rename, a deletion ("deleted here, but not in this browser's storage … comes back when the page is loaded again") or an import; a workspace another tab deleted meanwhile is said so ("… was deleted in another tab") and leaves the list. The dialog says these itself, under the list or under the hand-over file (`ws-list-outcome` / `ws-file-outcome`: a polite live line, a warning or failure as an alert, dismissible): a toast or a live region in <body> would be under the modal dialog, neither seen nor read while it is open. Esc in the rename field cancels the rename, not the dialog (the focus goes back to the row's Rename button, as after Save); Clear the list moves the focus to the empty list's note. Tests: `tests/e2e/workspaces.e2e.mjs` (offline; 1440 px, 375 px in Turkish and dark, 320 px).

Design: clean, professional dashboard; light/dark via tokens (`prefers-color-scheme` + manual toggle `data-theme`); system font stack + monospace for data; responsive to 360px (tables scroll horizontally inside their container, never the page); visible focus rings; `aria-live` progress; reduced motion honoured (scripted scrolls jump instead of animating: `ui/dom.scrollBehavior()`); keyboard accessible tabs; inline SVG icons (no icon fonts); status colors with text labels (not color-only). Large tables: paginate or incremental render (e.g. 200 rows + "show more").

## 7. CLI `cli/ssl_origin_scan.py` (Python ≥3.8, stdlib only, single file)

Purpose: definitively map hostnames → servers by TLS-probing inventory IPs **with SNI**, bypassing DNS/Cloudflare. Run from a host inside the network (jump box).
```
python3 ssl_origin_scan.py -t targets.txt [-t 10.0.0.0/24 -t web01.internal ...] (-n names.txt | -n host ... | --cert new-cert.pem) [--ports 443,8443] [--include-backends] [--workers 64] [--timeout 5] [--json out.json] [--csv out.csv] [--show-all] [--no-color]
    [--baseline previous.json [--fail-on-change]] [--warn-days N] [--notify URL [--notify-format F] [--notify-always] [--fail-on-notify-error]] [--estate] [--tls-audit]
    [-p 25/smtp,443,993 | a target 203.0.113.10:5432/postgres] [--profile web|mail|all]... [--cafile FILE]
python3 ssl_origin_scan.py bundle-check FILE [FILE ...] [-o DIR [--write-haproxy]] [--no-color]
```
- targets: same flexible inventory formats as the web app (name+ip lines, `NAME=IP` lines, hosts file, CSV, Ansible INI, JSON) + CIDR ranges (cap e.g. /16 with warning) + hostnames (resolved with getaddrinfo).
  - An address or host name with its own port (`203.0.113.10:8443`, `[2001:db8::1]:8443` — IPv6 needs the brackets —, `web01.example.net:8443`, `NAME=IP:PORT`; in `-t` and in files) is scanned on that port **instead of** `-p`; `-p` applies to every target written without one, and a target listed both ways gets both (`Server.ports`, `None` = the `-p` ports). A port outside 1–65535 or not a number, a bad address in brackets, a bracketed token that is no `[ADDRESS]:PORT` (`[2001:db8::1]8443`), an IPv6 zone id with a port (`[fe80::1%eth0]:8443`) and a CIDR / range with a port are a usage error on the command line and an `INVALID_IP` warning in a file — never silently dropped (in JSON too: such a value is a warning and the object's name is not resolved instead); a server name with a port (`web01.example.net:8443 203.0.113.10`) is a `PARSE` warning and the name is used without it; a host name with a port next to an address (`web01 203.0.113.10 db.example.net:5432`) is a `PARSE` warning and ignored (a host name is resolved only for an entry without an address; without a port there it is a hosts-file alias). A first-token `NAME=HOST[:PORT]` in a file is a target as in `-t` when HOST has a dot or a port is given (`user=root` stays a variable). A time of day in a line (`backup 10:30 203.0.113.10`, `time=10:30`) is ignored, as the web app does. In an Ansible INI context (a line under a `[group]` header or with an `ansible_*=` variable) a port on the first token, the host pattern (`203.0.113.11:2222`, `[2001:db8::5]:2222`, `badwolf.example.com:5309`), is Ansible's SSH port: the host is scanned on `-p` and a `PARSE` warning says so (§5.5, the same rule). `DUPLICATE_IP` compares endpoints, not bare addresses: one address on different ports for different servers is none. The JSON's `servers[].ports` lists the addresses with ports of their own; the "Scanning …" line and the summary header count ip:port endpoints then.
  - CSV headers follow §5.5: the same IP-column rule (`isIpKey`: gateway, DNS, NTP, iLO / iDRAC / IPMI / BMC, MAC, e-mail and URL columns are never server addresses, also in a file without an IP column, whose other columns are read for addresses: a subnet there is never swept), Turkish name and group headers (`Sunucu Adı`, `IP Adresi`, `Ortam`; accents and `ı` folded), the best-ranked name column, and plain heading lines (`hostname   ip`) skipped. A heading has two or more words and none with a dot or a digit group, so an EC2-style `ip-10-0-1-23.example.net`, `ipv6.example.com` or a lone `node` stays a host name. A value with `@` (an e-mail address) is a `PARSE` warning, never a host to resolve. As in the web app, a row's first cell makes it a comment (`#`, `;`, `//`), so a `;` row with an empty first cell (Excel in Turkish and other European locales) is a row and a `;` header may start with an empty cell; blank `;;` rows and Excel's leading `sep=;` line are skipped.
  - Unlike the web app, a row with a name but no IP is kept and its name resolved. A word without a digit, a dot or a colon in an IP column (`DHCP`, `N/A`, `TBD`, `-`) is no IP, as in the JSON reader; a host name there, or any word in an `ansible_host` column, is resolved instead of the name.
  - **Topology keys** (§5.5, read alike; `Server.tls_ports`, `terminates_tls`, `vips`, `nats`, `backends`): `ports=443,8443` (`tls_ports=` in JSON / YAML) scans the server's addresses written without a port on those ports instead of `-p` (an address with its own port keeps exactly that port: `Server.ports_for`, `endpoint_spec`); `terminates_tls=no` sets the server aside — never connected to, `ScanReport.skipped_backends` — unless `--include-backends`, except a load balancer passing TLS through with no server behind it terminating TLS (`servers_set_aside`: TLS would end nowhere, so the scan shows what answers there), and a run left with only such servers is a usage error naming the flag; a `vip=` / `nat=` address is not scanned itself, each server is scanned on its own addresses (add a VIP with `-t` to see what the active node serves); `backends=` may name a server of another `-t` file (`link_backends` runs once every file is read). A malformed value is a `TOPOLOGY` warning (`InventoryWarning.reason` as the web app names it), never a dropped server; the inventory-wide checks (`noTermination`, `vipMixed`, `cycle`, `ownedAddress`), the near misses and the address-only lines that hand their keys to a named server are the web app's (§5.5). With any key the summary opens with "By load balancer: N" (`render_topology`: each load balancer with its status and role — "terminates TLS: install the certificate here" or "passes TLS through (terminates_tls=no): no certificate here", its VIPs — and its backends: "re-encrypts: needs the certificate too" or "plain HTTP, no certificate needed" (a load balancer of the next tier: "passes TLS through (terminates_tls=no): no certificate here"), "not scanned" with the flag that scans it; "TLS terminates nowhere - check the inventory" when no backend terminates it, on the load balancer's line and on each plain backend's — "plain HTTP (terminates_tls=no), yet the load balancer passes TLS through to it: TLS terminates nowhere - check the inventory", never "no certificate needed" (2026-10-09)), then each VIP with its holders ("install the certificate on both"; holders that disagree: "install the certificate on db01; db02 says terminates_tls=no - check the inventory"), the NAT pairs and the servers with `terminates_tls=no` outside a load balancer that were not scanned; every server line gets a `[…]` tag (`topology_tag`: `LB: …`, `behind …, re-encrypts`, `VIP … with …`, `NAT …`, `TLS ports …`). A `terminates_tls=no` server that answers TLS for the names (`--include-backends`, or a load balancer with TLS ending nowhere) never reads "no certificate needed": its line says it answers TLS although the inventory says plain HTTP - check the inventory, its tag "terminates_tls=no but answers TLS - check the inventory". The JSON adds `servers[].topology` (`terminatesTls`, `tlsPorts`, `vips`, `nats`, `backends`, `behind` — also for a backend without keys of its own), `skippedBackends` and `options.includeBackends`, only with topology keys, so an old inventory's report is unchanged. `--baseline`: an endpoint left out now for `terminates_tls=no` is `SKIPPED` ("not scanned now (terminates_tls=no; --include-backends scans it); was …"), listed but never counted by `--fail-on-change` or `--notify`: the inventory changed, not the server. `--compare` refuses `--include-backends`. Tests: `test_topology_scan.py` (fake connect / TLS) and the parity in `test_inventory_targets.py`.
- names: from files/args; `--cert FILE` adds the cert's SAN DNS names (wildcards: probe the base domain and any provided names under it) AND enables fingerprint comparison (served cert == new cert → "already updated").
  - `--cert` is repeatable (an RSA + ECDSA pair, several certificates renewed together): every file's names are probed and a served certificate that is any of them is UPDATED. With two different certificates or more (`ScanReport.several_new_certs`) the reports name the file a server serves: `(matches FILE)` in the summary's UPDATED groups and no-SNI line, `New certificate (FILE): …` in the header, `newCertFile` on each JSON result (null when none of them is served), `file` on each `newCertificates` entry, and a last CSV column `new_cert` (`NEW_CERT_CSV_COLUMN`). With one `--cert` (or the same one twice) every report is byte-identical to before. A `--cert` another `--cert` probably replaces (`replaced_new_certs`, the rule of certsets `replacedLeaves`: the same key algorithm, all of its names in the other, the other issued later) gets a warning, since a server still serving it would be UPDATED. `run_scan(new_cert_files={sha256: FILE})`; tests in `tests/python/test_several_certs.py`.
  - `--cert` text (PEM, bare base64) may be UTF-8, UTF-16 with a BOM or UTF-16LE without one, as PowerShell 5.1's `>` writes it, like `-t` / `-n` / `--exclude` files and `lib/x509.js`.
  - A CT precertificate (the poison extension, RFC 6962: the serial and names of the issued certificate in other bytes, which no server serves, so every server would be NEEDS_UPDATE) is refused as `--cert`, naming the serial of the certificate to give instead; a CA certificate that names no host (an intermediate, a root) gets a warning.
  - Internationalised names (in `-n`, `-t` and inventories) become punycode as in the web app (UTS #46 non-transitional, §5.3): `straße` → `xn--strae-oqa`, never IDNA 2003's `strasse`, which is another registrable name. `ς` stays `ς`; ZWJ / ZWNJ are kept only right after a virama, otherwise the name is invalid (a Persian ZWNJ name is given in its `xn--` form). Ideographic full stops (`。` `．` `｡`) separate labels as in the web app (mapped after lowercasing, so `ΑΣ。x` keeps a final `ς`, and never into a `*.` wildcard); Cherokee letters stay capital as UTS #46 maps them; a label that starts with a combining mark, carries an `xn--` prefix on non-ASCII text or mixes `ß` / `ς` with right-to-left letters is invalid.
- Phase 1: TCP connect check per ip:port (parallel) → skip closed. Phase 2: for each open ip:port × name: TLS handshake with SNI=name, `CERT_NONE`, permissive (`minimum_version` lowest supported, `set_ciphers('ALL:@SECLEVEL=0')` guarded by try), fetch DER via `getpeercert(binary_form=True)`, parse with a built-in minimal DER parser (subject CN, SAN DNS/IP, issuer CN/O, serial, notBefore/notAfter incl. GeneralizedTime, sha256 fingerprint). Also probe once with no SNI to learn the default cert.
  - Handshakes go name by name across the endpoints, and at most `MAX_PER_ENDPOINT` (4) run against one ip:port at a time, whatever `--workers` is: dozens of simultaneous connections from the jump host trip per-client connection limits (nginx stream `limit_conn`, HAProxy `src_conn_cur`, WAF appliances). A handshake waiting for its turn holds no worker thread. An endpoint whose last four handshakes all timed out (a tarpit, a balancer without a backend, an SNI router whose backend for the remaining names hangs) is not held to the cap, so it costs a few timeouts rather than one per four names; the cap is back once a handshake there ends otherwise.
  - Works rule: a name the server refuses (alert, close, reset) while other handshakes on the same ip:port complete is `NOT_HOSTED` "server refused this name". A close, reset or refused connection (no TLS alert) is first retried once, one handshake at a time per endpoint, so a limiter's resets never turn hosted names into `NOT_HOSTED`; a TLS alert is the server's answer and is not retried. A vhost that requires a client certificate (mutual TLS: HAProxy `verify required`, Apache `SSLVerifyClient require`) refuses no name: in TLS 1.2 it sends its certificate and a CertificateRequest before it aborts, and the row is judged by that certificate (kept with `SSLContext._msg_callback`), as a TLS 1.3 handshake, which completes on the client's side, is.
- **STARTTLS by port** (P1.10): what an endpoint speaks before TLS follows its port (`PORT_PROTOCOLS`): SMTP on 25 and 587 (EHLO then STARTTLS), IMAP on 143, POP3 on 110 (STLS), FTP on 21 (AUTH TLS), LDAP on 389 (the StartTLS extended request, OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.20037), XMPP on 5222 (the client stream's `<starttls/>`), PostgreSQL on 5432 (the SSLRequest `00000008 04d2162f`) and RDP on 3389 (an X.224 Connection Request in a TPKT carrying an RDP_NEG_REQ for PROTOCOL_SSL | PROTOCOL_HYBRID, `_RDP_REQUEST`; the Connection Confirm's RDP_NEG_RSP must select TLS or CredSSP — both start with the TLS handshake —, an RDP_NEG_FAILURE (`_RDP_FAILURES`: SSL_NOT_ALLOWED_BY_SERVER …), Standard RDP Security or no negotiation data is a `TLS_ERROR` saying so; checked against fake servers only, as no real one was at hand); every other port — 443 and the implicit-TLS 465, 993, 995, 636, 990 and 5223 — speaks TLS from the first byte. Each upgrade is a raw exchange (`starttls()`, `_starttls_*`: send the command, read one line or PDU, wrap the socket), so a minimal server that re-sends no CAPABILITY works; data before the go-ahead, or endless replies, is a `TLS_ERROR` that says the protocol. A port carries an explicit protocol after a slash — `-p 2525/smtp`, a target `203.0.113.10:2525/smtp` (that endpoint only), `25/tls` (TLS from the first byte), an inventory `ports=2525/smtp` — read by `ProtocolPort` (a port that prints, sorts and hashes as its number so it travels wherever ports do) and `endpoint_protocol()`; the protocols are `tls`, `smtp`, `imap`, `pop3`, `ftp`, `ldap`, `xmpp`, `postgres` and `rdp` (aliases `submission`, `pop`, `postgresql` / `pgsql`, `xmpp-client`, `ms-wbt-server`), any other word a usage error naming the token. `--profile web|mail|all` (repeatable, `PORT_PROFILES`, `resolve_ports`) scans a kind of server's ports instead of `-p`'s default 443: web 443, 8443; mail 25, 587, 465, 143, 993, 110, 995; all of those and 21, 990, 389, 636, 5222, 5223, 5432 and 3389. `-p` (now `None` by default) adds its own ports after the profiles' (a port in both once, the protocol `-p` writes winning); an inventory's `ports=` still replaces them for its server; `--compare` refuses it; the JSON's `options.ports` lists the result and `options.profiles` the profiles (only when given). The renewal-day statuses below apply unchanged, so mail, directory, chat and database servers are covered by the same scan and `--cert` / `--estate` / `--baseline` work as before; a server offering no STARTTLS is a `TLS_ERROR` saying so. `--compare` refuses a STARTTLS port (its HTTP GET needs TLS from the first byte). The JSON's `endpoints` entries carry a `protocol` field where STARTTLS was spoken (`_endpoint_dict`, absent on 443 and the implicit-TLS ports), additive so the `lib/estate.js` / `lib/verify.js` readers' version checks keep reading; the `tlsAudit` section always names each endpoint's protocol. An inventory's `ports=25,143,389,5432` — and `ports=3389` — is no "carries no TLS" warning now (the web app reads the same files, §5.5; `_PLAIN_PORTS` and lib/inventory.js `PLAIN_PORTS` lost 3389 together). Tests: `test_starttls_audit.py` (fake SMTP / IMAP / POP3 / FTP / LDAP / XMPP / PostgreSQL responders on 127.0.0.1 threads with fixture certs).
- Status per (server, port, name): `UPDATED` (serves the new cert), `NEEDS_UPDATE` (served cert covers the name but is not the new cert — show its expiry), `ORIGIN_CERT` (… a Cloudflare Origin CA certificate: issuer O `CloudFlare, Inc.` with OU / CN `CloudFlare Origin SSL [ECC ]Certificate Authority`, the real roots' DNs), `PRIVATE_CERT` (… a self-signed certificate — same subject and issuer DN and, when both are present, key identifier — or one issued by a CA given with `--private-ca FILE`: PEM / DER / P7B CA certificates, matched by issuer DN and AKI = SKI; every certificate of each file counts), `NOT_HOSTED` (served cert does not cover the name / only default cert), `TLS_ERROR`, `CLOSED`, `TIMEOUT`.
  - ORIGIN_CERT and PRIVATE_CERT apply only when the certificate is of another kind than every new one (`HostedClassifier`): rolling out an Origin CA (or self-signed / private-CA) certificate keeps the older ones of that family NEEDS_UPDATE, and a certificate with a new one's issuer DN is always NEEDS_UPDATE. `--strict-public` restores the old rule (all of them NEEDS_UPDATE). They are listed in their own summary sections with an explanation, in the JSON (`servers[].originCert` / `privateCert`, `summary.serversWithOriginCert` / `serversWithPrivateCert`, `certificates{}.kind` / `privateCa`, `options.strictPublic` / `privateCa`) and in the CSV `status` column; the roll-up order is NEEDS_UPDATE > UPDATED > ORIGIN_CERT > PRIVATE_CERT > TLS_ERROR > … `CLOSED` comes only from the phase-1 port check; a connection refused during phase 2 (the port was open a moment before: a connection limiter, fail2ban, a restart) is a `TLS_ERROR`, so such a server is listed under handshake errors, never as "not hosting any of the names".
- **Trust** (every scan; closes the wave 6 follow-up "full TLS chain validation"; `check_trust`, phase 3 of `run_scan`): the scan's handshakes read whatever is served and trust nothing, so after them one verifying handshake is made per distinct served certificate, chain sent and name — the rows whose certificate covers the name (UPDATED, NEEDS_UPDATE, ORIGIN_CERT, PRIVATE_CERT), keyed by the leaf's SHA-256, `TlsResult.chain_sha256` (`chain_digest` of the certificates as sent, `_chain_ders`: Python 3.10+; none on 3.8 / 3.9, where the leaf and the name alone key it) and the SNI, against the first endpoint that served it (after STARTTLS in its protocol), `--workers` at a time. `_verify_side` (shared with `--compare`) wraps the socket with `trust_context`: `verify_context(True)` — `ssl.create_default_context()`, CERT_REQUIRED and the name checked, VERIFY_X509_STRICT taken off, VERIFY_X509_TRUSTED_FIRST — or, with `--cafile FILE`, only that file's CAs (`create_default_context(cafile=FILE)`; one that cannot be read, or holds no certificate, is a usage error before anything is sent: `load_trust_context`; the `--tls-audit` chain check and `--compare` use it too). A covering certificate a `--private-ca` issued counts as trusted within its dates (`issued by a --private-ca`). Not trusted, `trust_detail` names OpenSSL's verify code (`TRUST_DETAILS`): `missing intermediate or private CA (code 20)`, `missing intermediate (code 21)`, `self-signed (code 18)`, `a root this machine does not trust (code 19)`, `expired (code 10)`, `not yet valid (code 9)`, `hostname mismatch (code 62)`, else the verify message with its code; a handshake that could not be made is no verdict (null, with why). `trust_verifier(cafile, private_cas, context)` is the default `verify_fn`; `run_scan(verify_fn=…)` injects one, and a scan whose `tls_fn` was injected (tests) checks trust only with an injected `verify_fn` (`ScanReport.trust_checked`, `trust_store`: `system`, `windows` — `trust_store_name` — or `cafile`, and `cafile`, the file's base name). Reports (only when it ran, so the reports of a scan without it are as before): every JSON row `certTrusted` (true / false / null where it was not asked: no certificate covering the name, a failed handshake, the no-SNI probe) and `trustDetail`, `options.trust: {store, cafile}`; the CSV adds `cert_trusted` (yes / no / empty) and `trust_detail` last (`TRUST_CSV_COLUMNS`, `trust_cells`); the summary prints `untrusted: <detail>` in red under each group a name of which is served with an untrusted chain — `untrusted (Windows store may be incomplete): …` on Windows without `--cafile` (`untrusted_text`, `WINDOWS_STORE_NOTE`: the Windows store fetches the roots it lacks on demand) — and `Not trusted by <store>: N names on M endpoints` (N distinct names) before the results line (`render_trust_line`); `--estate` (below) carries each endpoint's verdict and flags the certificate `untrusted`. With `--baseline`, when both runs checked trust (`_checked_trust`: `options.trust`): a name now served with an untrusted chain where the baseline trusted it or had no verdict is `untrusted` (tag UNTRUSTED, counted, bad; `_trust_change`, next to the row's own change), trusted again `trusted` (TRUSTED, good) — a row whose handshake failed in the baseline run has the verdict it had before (`_verdicts_before_failure`: the baseline's own FAILED change keeps the row as it was), so a row back from a failed night with the chain it had says RECOVERED only, and one that failed with no verdict known is compared with none —; the change's `after` carries `trustStore` (`_trust_store_of`: the store of the verdict) and its words say whose verdict it is (`_untrusted_by`: `not trusted by this machine`, `not trusted by this machine (Windows store may be incomplete)` for the Windows store, `not trusted by the CAs of --cafile`); `baseline.trustCheckedIn` and a note when only one run checked it; a row's `certTrusted` that is not true, false or null is a damaged baseline. PagerDuty pages UNTRUSTED as critical (`PAGERDUTY_CRITICAL_TAGS`; `pagerduty_severity`: error for a verdict of the Windows store without --cafile, which may lack a root it has not fetched yet — Python never triggers its on-demand fetch) and resolves it once the name's chain is trusted (`_problem_over`; a run without the check says nothing). Tests: `tests/python/test_trust_check.py` (a fake verifier over a fake fleet: once per certificate, chain and name, a leaf sent with another chain asked again, STARTTLS passed on, the JSON, the CSV and the summary with each store's words, a name on two endpoints counted once, UNTRUSTED / TRUSTED with each store's words and PagerDuty's severity (error for the Windows store), a row back from a failed night, the notes, PagerDuty, the estate; a `--cafile` that cannot be read; `--cafile`, `--private-ca` and a hostname mismatch against a local TLS server).
- Output: human-readable summary grouped by server ("servers that need the new certificate: N") with colors (auto-disabled when not a TTY/`--no-color`/`NO_COLOR`), plus `--json` / `--csv`. Exit code 0 unless usage error (2) or a report file that could not be written after the scan (3); `--fail-on-needs-update` → exit 1 when any NEEDS_UPDATE (for CI; ORIGIN_CERT and PRIVATE_CERT servers count only with `--strict-public`); `--fail-on-change` → 4 and `--fail-on-notify-error` → 5 (see Monitoring below). When several apply: 3, then 5, then 4, then 1.
  - A `--json` / `--csv` file that cannot be written (missing directory, read-only, locked by Excel) is a usage error before the scan; the check truncates nothing and leaves no file behind.
  - If a report still cannot be written after the scan, the error is printed, the other report and the summary are still written, and the exit code is 3 (it wins over 1).
- Robust: Ctrl-C handling, per-connection timeout, thread pool, IPv6 support, no stack traces for expected errors.
- Untrusted certificates: any server in a swept range can answer with any certificate.
  - A certificate the parser cannot read (malformed, out-of-range times, oversized OIDs) becomes a `TLS_ERROR` row (`unparseable certificate: ...`), or a `PARSE_ERROR` for `--cert`, never a crash.
  - The summary and the warnings escape control, format and line-separator characters of certificate text and inventory names (`\x1b[2K` is printed as the text `\x1b[2K`), so a subject cannot move the cursor, rewrite lines or set the window title. The JSON keeps the exact values.
  - CSV text cells follow the web app's `toCsv` rule (§5.16): a cell starting with `=` `+` `-` `@` TAB or CR gets a leading `'`, so a CN such as `=HYPERLINK(...)` stays text in Excel. Control characters and bidi embeddings / overrides / isolates are escaped; ZWNJ, ZWJ, the soft hyphen and LRM / RLM of real names stay in a file, and only `--csv -` escapes everything the summary does. Numbers (port, days left) are left as they are.
- `--exclude ADDR [ADDR ...]` (repeatable) takes IPs, CIDRs (v4 / v6), ranges, `-` for stdin, or a file of them (`#` comments).
  - Host names are refused (exit 2).
  - IPv4-mapped addresses match both ways.
  - It is applied after names are resolved and before any connection.
  - Reported in the summary, in the JSON (`excluded[]`, `summary.excludedAddresses`, `options.exclude`) and in the CSV (rows with `probe=excluded`, status `EXCLUDED`). A rule that matches nothing is a warning.
- Numeric "host names" that the resolver would read as IPv4 are refused: all digits, hex, octal, dotted numeric, full-width digits, ideographic dots, a trailing dot (`2026092401`, `127.1`, `0x7f.0x1`).
  - In `-t`, NAME=IP and `-n` this is exit 2; from a file, the entry is skipped with a warning. They never reach the resolver.
  - IPv4 parts with a leading zero (`010.0.0.1`) are refused as ambiguous.
  - A typo'd range or CIDR (`10.0.0.5-300`, `10.0.0.5-9x`, `10.0.0.5-09`, `10.0.0.0/33`) is a valid LDH name but never resolved: exit 2 on the command line ("not a valid IP range / CIDR", not "file not found"), `INVALID_IP` in a file. A name whose last label or range end starts with a letter (`10.0.0.5-web.example.com`, `192.0.2.1-db`) is still a host name.
  - 0.0.0.0/8, multicast and broadcast addresses are never scanned.
- Monitoring between visits, for cron / scheduled tasks (no infrastructure): `load_baseline()`, `compare_reports()`, `expiring_certificates()`, `build_monitor()` → `MonitorResult`, `build_notification()`, `send_notification()`.
  - `--baseline FILE` is a previous `--json` report (UTF-8 or UTF-16 with a BOM), read and checked before the scan: a file that is not JSON, not a report of this tool (`"tool": "ssl_origin_scan"`), written by another major version, or with a malformed row (`ip`, `port`, `status`, `probe`, `certSha256`) or a `names` / `newCertificates` / `options.ports` that is not a list is a usage error (exit 2) naming the problem. `--baseline -` is refused. The same file may be given to `--json`: it is read before the scan and replaced after it (a temporary file in the same directory renamed over it, so a write that fails keeps the last baseline whole; a directory that does not take a new file is exit 2 before the scan), and while it does not exist (the first run) there is nothing to compare (`baseline.missing: true`); a missing baseline that is not also the `--json` file is exit 2. The same file as `--csv` is exit 2 (a CSV would overwrite it and cannot be compared).
  - `compare_reports(before, after)` compares per (ip, port, name); addresses are normalised (`2001:0DB8::5` = `2001:db8::5`), servers sharing an address give one change listing them all. Each change is `{kind, scope, transition, servers, ip, port, probe, name, before, after, certChanged}`:
    - scope `name`: a name probed in only one report (`appeared` / `disappeared`, with its status counts); its rows are not listed one by one;
    - scope `endpoint`: an ip:port scanned in only one report (`after.status: EXCLUDED` when `--exclude` removed it) or whose port state moved (OPEN / CLOSED / TIMEOUT, `transition` as for rows), with the name counts of the open side;
    - scope `row` (endpoint open in both): a status that moved (`status`, `transition` = `failed` to TLS_ERROR / TIMEOUT / CLOSED, `recovered` from one, `failing` from one of them to another, `regressed` UPDATED → another covering status, `updated` the reverse, `unhosted` covering → NOT_HOSTED, `hosted` the reverse, else `changed`), another served certificate with the same status (`cert`, by SHA-256 fingerprint; for covering rows only, the no-SNI probe's included — a NOT_HOSTED row's fallback certificate, with or without SNI, is not a change: proxies such as Traefik or ingress-nginx make theirs anew on every restart, a default vhost often carries another site's certificate that renews on its own schedule), or a row only one report has.
    - "Covering" is UPDATED, NEEDS_UPDATE, ORIGIN_CERT, PRIVATE_CERT and any status this version does not know (a later version's certificate kinds), so reports of other minor versions compare (a report from before ORIGIN_CERT / PRIVATE_CERT compares too: a server that was NEEDS_UPDATE there and is PRIVATE_CERT now is a `changed` status); unknown probe kinds are skipped.
    - A `failing` move (CLOSED ↔ TIMEOUT, TLS_ERROR ↔ TIMEOUT) served nothing either way, and on a sweep with a short `--timeout` a refused connection and a timeout can take turns: it is listed (summary, JSON, message — after the other changes: `build_monitor` orders them once with `order_changes()`, so every cap cuts these moves first) but does not count (`counts_as_change()`, `notable_changes()`): it never triggers `--notify` or `--fail-on-change`, nor holds a baseline back.
  - `--warn-days N` (0–3650, off by default) lists served certificates that cover a probed name (covering rows, also the no-SNI probe) and expire within N days or have expired, soonest first: `{sha256, subjectCN, issuer, serialHex, notAfter, daysLeft, expired, isNewCert, endpoints: [{server, ip, port, names, defaultCert}]}`.
  - Output: the summary opens with "Changes since the baseline (FILE, scan of …): N" (a tag per change — FAILED, REGRESSED, UNHOSTED, GONE, UNTRUSTED in red; TRUSTED in green; RECOVERED, UPDATED in green; HOSTED in green only when the name is now served with the new certificate, else yellow; NEW; CERT, CHANGED in yellow; FAILING dimmed — at most 50 without `--show-all`, plus a note counting the FAILING moves and notes when the ports or the `--cert` differ from the baseline's) and "Served certificates expiring within N days". The `--json` document gains `baseline` (`{file, missing, version, startedAt, finishedAt, portsAdded, portsRemoved, newCertificateChanged}`) and `changes` with `--baseline`, `expiring` and `options.warnDays` with `--warn-days`; without them it is unchanged. `--fail-on-change` (needs `--baseline`) exits 4 when there is any change that counts. A reader of the summary that goes away (`| head`, `| grep -q`) is not an error: the rest of stdout goes to the null device and the notification and the baseline still follow; stdout failing otherwise (a full disk behind `> file`) is an error line and exit 3, after them.
  - `--notify URL`, or `DOMAINSCOPE_NOTIFY_URL` so the URL stays out of the shell history, POSTs a short summary when something changed or expires (after every run with `--notify-always`). The format follows the URL (`--notify-format auto|slack|teams|discord|telegram|googlechat|json|pagerduty|ntfy` overrides it; PagerDuty and ntfy below): Slack incoming webhooks and Discord's `…/slack` endpoint → `{text}` (`& < >` escaped, the lines in a code block, so certificate text never becomes a mention or a link); Slack Workflow Builder webhooks (`hooks.slack.com/triggers/…`) get the same `{text}`, which the workflow reads as a variable named `text`; Teams incoming webhooks (`*.webhook.office.com`, `outlook.office.com`) and Power Automate / Logic Apps workflows (`*.logic.azure.com`, `*.api.powerplatform.com`) → a message with one Adaptive Card of plain TextRuns; Discord `/api/webhooks/` and `/api/v10/webhooks/` → `{content, allowed_mentions: {parse: []}}`; Telegram `https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/sendMessage?chat_id=<id>` → `{chat_id, text}` with `chat_id` moved from the query into the body; Google Chat space webhooks (`chat.googleapis.com`) → `{text}` like Slack's, but with `<` turned into the lookalike `‹` instead of escaped (Chat reads `<users/all>` as a mention and does not document decoding `&lt;`); any other URL → generic JSON `{tool, version, title, text, finishedAt, summary, baseline (its `file` as a base name, never the local path), changes (≤ 500), changesTotal, warnDays, expiring (≤ 50 certificates, each with ≤ 20 endpoints and `endpointsTotal`), expiringTotal}`. Chat texts fit the service's limit (Discord 2,000, Telegram 4,096) with at most 20 changes and 10 certificates, then "… and N more"; every line is cut at 400 characters and the footer names the ports as ranges (`443,8000-9023`), at most 8 of them, then "+N more".
  - The URL is checked before the scan (http / https, no spaces; a Telegram URL needs `/bot…/sendMessage` and `chat_id`; non-ASCII in its path or query is sent percent-encoded as UTF-8, `ascii_url()`) and is a credential: it is never printed or logged — only its host — and error texts and response bodies are redacted (`redact_url`: the URL with and without its user info, the path, query and fragment, the query values, the path segments that may be tokens — 8+ characters or a digit, other than the services' path words such as `services`, `webhooks`, `sendMessage` and API versions such as `v10`, as written, decoded and percent-encoded, and for Telegram's `bot<token>` also the token alone and its part after the `:` — the user name and password, and the Basic `Authorization` value made of them, base64 included). `user:password@` in the URL is sent as HTTP Basic authentication (`split_credentials`); urllib never sees it, since it would read `password@host` as a port and print it. `http://` to a non-loopback host is a warning. `urllib` only, certificate-verified HTTPS, the system proxy settings, no redirects (a redirected POST would arrive as a GET), 10 s timeout, one retry after 2 s (or a 429's Retry-After, ≤ 10 s) for network errors, 5xx and 429 — a 4xx is the webhook's answer. A failed notification is an `error:` line on stderr (also with `-q`) and changes the exit code only with `--fail-on-notify-error` (5); a delivered one prints "Notification sent (format, host)" unless `-q`.
  - When the `--json` file is also the baseline, the notification goes out before the file is replaced. If a message that carried changes is not delivered (or Ctrl-C stops it), the file keeps the previous report and stderr says so ("kept the previous baseline in FILE …: the N changes will be reported again on the next run"), so an outage of the chat service never loses a change; a message with only expiring certificates does not hold the baseline back, since they are listed again on every run. The cron example writes the summary to a file (`-q > last.txt`), so cron mails only errors.
  - PagerDuty, ntfy and a signed JSON webhook, as the headless runner's (§9):
    - `pagerduty` (detected for events.pagerduty.com and events.eu.pagerduty.com; the URL needs `routing_key`, which moves from the query into each event; `pagerduty_plan`, `pagerduty_events`): Events API v2 events, one POST each. A `trigger` per change that counts with a red tag (FAILED, REGRESSED, UNHOSTED, GONE, UNTRUSTED of the trust check: critical) and per certificate of `--warn-days` (EXPIRED, severity `critical`, or EXPIRES; `error` for the rest; `PAGERDUTY_CRITICAL_TAGS` also names the runner's registration, delegation and trust tags): `{routing_key, event_action, dedup_key, payload: {summary (≤ 1,024), source: 'domainscope:scan', severity, component: target, group: 'scan', custom_details: {tag, item, before, after, run: null}}, client: 'DomainScope'}`. `dedup_key` (`pagerduty_dedup_key`) is the first 32 hex characters of SHA-256 of `scan|target|item|tag`: target is the name (scope `name`) or the ip:port endpoint, item a row's name (`(no SNI)` for the probe without one); an expiring certificate's are its CN and SHA-256. At most 50 events a run (`NOTIFY_MAX_EVENTS`), triggers first: the triggers cut are said on stderr, the resolves cut stay open with `over` and go with the next run.
    - The JSON report keeps the keys triggered and not resolved, `notify.open: [{key, target, item, tag, since, over?}]` (at most 500, `PAGERDUTY_MAX_OPEN`, the oldest dropped; a run without a PagerDuty URL carries them as they are; `open_keys_of` drops a malformed entry). The next run with that report as `--baseline` sends a `resolve` for each open key whose problem is over in its own report (`pagerduty_plan(…, doc=report_to_dict(report))`, `_problem_over` over `_report_where(doc)`, indexed once): FAILED once the row or endpoint answers again, REGRESSED once the name is served with the new certificate (UPDATED), UNHOSTED once a certificate covering the name is served again, GONE once it is back; a certificate's key (RENEW-NOW, MOVED-UP, CA-NOTICE, REVOKED of `--ari` / `--revocation`: the item is its SHA-256, severity critical for REVOKED) once the endpoint serves no more of it (renewed or replaced) or is no longer scanned, never while it is served and never while nothing was read from the endpoint; a row whose name is no longer probed or whose endpoint is no longer scanned, an endpoint no longer scanned; for an expiring certificate, a run with `--warn-days` no longer lists it (renewed or replaced). Never because another change came by: a handshake that fails or a port that closes one night says nothing of the certificate a name is served with, so a REGRESSED stays open through it (without the report, nothing but an expiry is decided). A key triggered again keeps its `since`. The keys the report keeps are those delivered (`pagerduty_open_after(plan, triggered, resolved)`: the events before the first that failed; the JSON is rendered after the notification). A run whose PagerDuty event was not delivered keeps the previous baseline, as an undelivered message does — with its `notify.open` replaced by the keys open after the run when events went out (`_with_open_keys`, written whole; "…; the PagerDuty incidents still open are noted in it").
    - `ntfy` (ntfy.sh, or `--notify-format ntfy` for a self-hosted server; `build_ntfy`): the message's lines as plain text, at most 4,000 bytes of UTF-8 (`NTFY_MAX_BYTES`, `_fit_lines` measuring bytes), with `Title` (RFC 2047 when it is not ASCII), `Priority` 4 when a change is bad or a certificate expires (else 3), `Tags: warning`, and `Authorization: Bearer $DOMAINSCOPE_NTFY_TOKEN` when that is set and the URL has no user info of its own.
    - The json format is signed when `DOMAINSCOPE_NOTIFY_SECRET` is set (surrounding whitespace ignored; `notify_request`, `sign_body`): `X-DomainScope-Timestamp` (Unix seconds, from the CLI's clock `_utcnow`) and `X-DomainScope-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + body)>` over the exact bytes sent. The ntfy token, the secret, an ntfy topic and a PagerDuty routing key are redacted from error texts like the URL (`redact_url(text, url, extra)`), an answer's reason and status text before they are cut at 200 characters (`_response_detail(raw, redact)`), and an answer cut at the 512 bytes read without what it ends with that begins a secret (`_redact_with(text, secrets, cut)`).
  - Tests: `BaselineTests`, `ExpiryTests`, `ChangeSummaryTests`, `NotifyFormatTests`, `NotifyDeliveryTests` (a local `http.server` capturing each format's payload, retries, timeouts, redaction, Basic authentication from the URL, a non-ASCII URL, a failed delivery keeping the baseline for the next run), `NotifyChannelTests` (PagerDuty and ntfy detected and checked, the signature and the dedup key against known answers shared with `tests/js/ds-notify.test.js`, ntfy's message and its byte cut, a PagerDuty trigger and then a resolve over the test fleet, the 50-event budget and the open keys, a handshake that times out or a port closed one night ending no REGRESSED key, the keys kept as delivered, an answer echoing a secret across the 200-character cut or the 512 bytes read; through a local webhook: PagerDuty down (exit 5, the baseline kept), then delivered, then every incident resolved; a first trigger delivered before PagerDuty failed (the kept baseline notes it, the fleet back resolves it), ntfy with its token and a refused message redacted, the signed JSON at the CLI's clock), `MonitorCliTests` (exit codes, the same file as baseline and report, a writable directory, usage errors, FAILING moves, a summary reader that goes away, the documented commands) and `MonitorIntegrationTests` (two runs against real local TLS servers sharing one state file).
- `--estate`: an inventory of every certificate served; no `--cert` needed, no name needed either. Every ip:port is asked without SNI and for every `-n` name, every `--cert` name and every host name among the targets (`inventory_names`: a server named by a host name, a target given by host name; plain labels, addresses and numeric names are not). The scan and the result rows are the usual ones; `estate_from_report(doc, now)` (on the report dict, like `expiring_certificates`) gives the `estate` section of the JSON (`options.estate: true`; shape and rules: §5.48, which `lib/estate.js` mirrors exactly — `tests/fixtures/estate` holds reports whose `estate` both must reproduce). The summary (`render_estate`) replaces the per-server one: what was scanned, the certificates by expiry bucket and kind, then "Same name, different certificates" (OLDER marks the stale one), "Same key on several hosts or certificates" (addresses and certificates per key; NEEDS A LOOK where `shared_key_needs_look`: 2+ certificates or `SHARED_KEY_WIDE_HOSTS` = 5 addresses), "Weak keys or signatures", "Not trusted by <store>" (when the scan checked trust: the certificates an endpoint serves with an untrusted chain, each reason and where, the Windows note), "Covering none of the names asked" (left out when no name was asked, which a line says), and every certificate, soonest expiry first (key, signature, SHA-256 and SPKI prefixes, names, where it is served — at most `MAX_SUMMARY_ENDPOINTS` per list without `--show-all`), and the endpoints that gave no certificate (listed with `--show-all`). `--csv` writes the inventory instead of the result rows (`render_estate_csv`, `ESTATE_CSV_COLUMNS`: one row per certificate, endpoint and server; the same spreadsheet-safe cells). `--baseline`, `--warn-days`, `--notify` and the exit codes work as without it. Every `certificates{}` entry (with or without `--estate`) carries `spkiSha256`, the SHA-256 of its SubjectPublicKeyInfo.
- `--tls-audit` (P1.11): after the scan, a pass over every endpoint where a handshake completed (`audit_targets`, up to `--workers`, `MAX_PER_ENDPOINT` at one endpoint, each check its own handshake asking for the endpoint's first hosted name, in that endpoint's protocol). Per endpoint it records which TLS versions it accepts (1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, each offered alone by pinning `minimum_version` = `maximum_version`), whether it accepts weak cipher suites (`WEAK_CIPHER_GROUPS`: NULL `eNULL`, anonymous `aNULL`, export `EXP`, RC4, DES, 3DES — one family at a time via `set_ciphers`, TLS 1.2 at most) and which certificate key types it serves (RSA `aRSA`, ECDSA `aECDSA`, told apart by offering only the suites one key type signs; TLS 1.2, since Python cannot narrow TLS 1.3 signature algorithms, so a TLS 1.3-only endpoint cannot be asked one key type). Each check is `accepted` / `refused` / `untested` / `failed`; whatever the local OpenSSL or LibreSSL cannot offer (`NO_PROTOCOLS_AVAILABLE`, `NO_CIPHERS_AVAILABLE` — TLS 1.3 on LibreSSL 2.8, RC4 / 3DES on OpenSSL 3) is `untested`, never `refused`, and listed under "not tested" with the library name. Then the chain (`check_chain`, `chain_probe`; `audit_endpoint(..., chain_attempt, private_cas, now)` takes a stand-in): one handshake for the endpoint's name with `verify_context()` (ssl.create_default_context: this machine's trust store, the name checked when there is one; VERIFY_X509_STRICT, on from Python 3.13, taken off since clients do not apply it; VERIFY_X509_TRUSTED_FIRST set, as clients stop at the first certificate they trust), and, when that fails verification, one with the permissive scan context to read what it sends — when that one fails too, OpenSSL's verdict stands, `error` says why and each note adds that the chain could not be read. `analyze_chain(trusted, verify_code, verify_message, sent, leaf, built, sni, private_cas, now) -> ChainCheck { status: trusted|untrusted|untested, problems (CHAIN_PROBLEMS, the breaking ones before CHAIN_WARNINGS), notes (a sentence each), verifyCode, verifyMessage, sent, privateCa }`: from the certificates sent (`get_unverified_chain`, public on 3.13, the SSL object's on 3.10–3.12; `CAN_READ_CHAIN`, else the leaf alone and `untestable.chain` says so) the leaf's dates, the issuing path (`issued_by`: names and key identifiers, signatures never; in a trusted chain it follows the one OpenSSL built, `get_verified_chain`: at each step the issuer OpenSSL used, else another copy of one of its CAs — the same subject and key, a cross-sign —, else the first sent), an expired certificate on it (`expired-chain`), the order (`wrong-order`: the leaf first, then each issuer), a root sent (`extra-root`, every self-signed one sent: "the roots … are sent too"), certificates no part of it (`unrelated`; other copies of a CA on the path or of one OpenSSL used, and what issued those copies, are part of it), in a trusted chain an expired certificate the chain does without (`expired-extra`, a warning: a cross-signed copy of the root OpenSSL trusted, as the AddTrust and DST Root CA X3 cross-signs expired, a CA sent twice, what lies past that root — only old clients that build through it fail; a copy of an intermediate whose current copy came from this machine's store stays `expired-chain`), and a missing intermediate — the leaf sent alone while OpenSSL found no issuer (verify code 20 / 21), or one OpenSSL took from this machine's store (`get_verified_chain`) that the server did not send, a cross-signed copy (the same subject and key) counting as sent; from OpenSSL's code: `name-mismatch` (62), `self-signed` (18), `untrusted-root` (19, or 20 with a chain complete up to a CA whose issuer this machine lacks — a private CA, or on Windows a public root not fetched yet), `unknown-issuer` (20 when the chain cannot be read but the leaf can; "Python 3.10 and later tell which" only where `CAN_READ_CHAIN` is false), `expired` / `not-yet-valid` (by the leaf's dates), `untrusted` (any other, and 20 / 21 with nothing read at all: its message). A chain a `--private-ca` issued (any certificate on the path, or the leaf being one) is trusted through it, its dates still counting; a missing intermediate stays when that CA is no root. Last the fleet (`serial_mismatches(report, audits)`, in `TlsAudit.mismatches`): per name, the certificates served (the scan's hosted rows, and the audit's RSA / ECDSA handshakes for the name an endpoint was asked for, `AuditCheck.cert`, not in the JSON) grouped by key type (`KEY_TYPE_LABELS`, `_key_type`) and kind family (`_kind_family`: public / Origin CA / private) — by kind family alone where the audit tried both key types at the endpoints serving the name, none serves it with both and no RSA + ECDSA pair of `--cert` covers it (`_pair_covers`): the renewal changed the key type (the scan alone cannot tell that from a pair, so without the audit's key types it stays none); a group of two or more is a mismatch `{ name, keyType /* the newest certificate's */, keyTypeChanged, kind, certificates: [{ sha256, serialHex, keyType, issuer, notBefore, notAfter, older, endpoints: [{ ip, port, protocol, servers, behind /* the load balancers whose backends= name a server */, vips }] }] }`, newest first, `older` when another was issued later. Fleet summary (`audit_summary`): the endpoints still accepting TLS 1.0 / 1.1 (`LEGACY_VERSIONS`), the ones accepting weak suites, the ones serving one half of an expected RSA + ECDSA pair (`_expected_pairs`: a name another endpoint serves with both, or that an RSA and an ECDSA `--cert` cover), `chainsChecked`, `chainsBroken`, `chainProblems` (each endpoint with a problem: status, problems, notes, verifyMessage, privateCa) and `serialMismatches`; `render_tls_audit` prints "Certificate chain not trusted or incomplete", "Chain sent with extra or misordered certificates" and `render_serial_mismatches` ("One name served with different certificates across the endpoints", OLDER marking the certificate a renewal left behind, each endpoint with "behind LB" / "VIP"; a changed key type reads "RSA to ECDSA: the key type changed, no endpoint serves both", each certificate with its key type). The JSON gains `tlsAudit` (`library`, `untestable` — `chain` too where Python cannot read what a server sends —, `summary`, `endpoints[]` each with every check's outcome and its `chain`) and `options.tlsAudit: true`; the result rows, the per-server summary and `--csv` are unchanged (the audit prints after them, `MAX_AUDIT_LINES` per finding without `--show-all`), so an old reader is unaffected. Works with `--estate`, `--baseline` and `--notify`. Tests: `test_starttls_audit.py` `FakeAuditTests` (findings, fleet summary, JSON) and `LocalAuditTests` (real local servers, version-pinning skipped where the local OpenSSL lacks a version); `test_tls_audit_fleet.py` — RDP's negotiation over a socket pair and a scan of local RDP servers, `--profile`, `analyze_chain` over the bundle-check and chainfix PKIs (complete, the leaf alone with the CA's URL, an intermediate this machine had, a cross-signed copy, a root this machine lacks, order, a root sent, an unrelated certificate, dates, a name, self-signed, Python before 3.10, a --private-ca) and the cross-sign PKI of `gen_cross_fixtures.sh` (`cross_*`: an expired cross-signed copy of the trusted root sent in either order, with and without that root and the old one, and an expired copy of an intermediate sent instead of or next to the current one), the audit with chain stand-ins (summary, JSON, text, a reading handshake that fails), the fleet check (a pool member behind its load balancer, an RSA + ECDSA pair and an Origin CA certificate that are none, the RSA half the audit's handshake brings, a renewal from RSA to ECDSA that missed a pool member) and real local servers sending the chain complete, alone and reversed to a client that trusts the test root, and the expired cross-sign in either order to one that trusts the Cross Root.
- `--ari` / `--revocation` (the renewal radar, §5.94; with a scan and `--estate`, refused with `--compare`): after the scan, each certificate served (by SHA-256) is asked about once. `--ari`: its CA (`ari_ca_for_issuer` over the issuer DN: Let's Encrypt, Google Trust Services, ZeroSSL, Sectigo, SSL.com by key type — `ARI_DIRECTORIES`, the runner's table, §3) through `AriClient` (the directory's `renewalInfo` read once a run and only on that CA's ARI host, then `GET <renewalInfo>/<ari_cert_id>`; `STATUS_WORKERS` at a time; 404 `not-found`; a CA that answered 429 or 503 with Retry-After not asked again in the run; the baseline's record carried while its `retryAfter` lies ahead), recording `ari: { ca, certId, start, end, explanationURL, checkedAt, retryAfter, status, error, carried? }`. `--revocation`: `RevocationChecker` reads each CRL distribution point once (`http_get`, ≤ `CRL_MAX_BYTES` = 20 MB, `CRL_TIMEOUT` = 15 s for the whole download — `http_get` reads the body a socket read at a time against a `time.monotonic()` deadline, so a server that trickles it is a `timeout`, as the runner's —), `parse_crl` with the serials asked, `crl_status` as lib/crl.js crlStatus (another CA's, delta, an unknown critical extension, another scope — an IDP URL urllib cannot split is compared as text, as lib/crl.js `sameUrl` —, stale: `unknown`, the next point tried; a CRL it cannot judge for any other reason is `unknown` with error `unknown`, never the scan lost), recording `revocation: { status, reason, reasonCode, time, crl, checkedAt, thisUpdate, nextUpdate, signature: 'not-verified' | null, error }` — Python's stdlib cannot check the CRL's signature, and every line says "CRL signature not verified". The summary's "Renewal windows and revocation" section lists them revoked first, then the windows open or past (`render_cert_status`); the JSON gives each `certificates{}` entry `ari` / `revocation` and `options.ari` / `options.revocation`; the scan's and `--estate`'s CSV add `ARI_CSV_COLUMNS` (`ari_start`, `ari_end`, `ari_explanation`, `ari_error`) and `REVOCATION_CSV_COLUMNS` (`revocation`, `revoked_at`, `revocation_reason`, `revocation_error`) after their own (`estate_status_columns`); `--estate` adds "Renewal windows and revocation: N revoked, N to renew now" and each certificate's records. With `--baseline` (`_status_changes`, compare_reports): RENEW-NOW (the window opened or ended since the baseline's run — the window its answer gave, at its `finishedAt`, never at the answer's `checkedAt`, which an answer carried past its Retry-After keeps —, or a certificate first seen in it, an endpoint new to the baseline's too), MOVED-UP (it starts more than a day earlier), CA-NOTICE (an explanationURL the baseline's answers did not carry) and REVOKED (a served certificate on its CRL, not before) — all counted, red. Tests: `tests/python/test_ari_revocation.py` (the CertID, the CA mapping, CRL parsing and verdicts over the `crl_*` fixtures, the ARI client and revocation checker over fake fetches, `http_get` against a local server and one that trickles its body, three nights through `run_main`, RENEW-NOW once across an answer carried past a run (asked, carried, asked), a CRL whose IDP URL urllib cannot split and one `crl_status` cannot judge (the scan kept), a carried answer's status escaped for the terminal, the estate with both and its CSV, refused with `--compare`).
- `bundle-check FILE...` (the first argument, or after `--no-color` / `--write-haproxy` only — `BUNDLE_LEADING_FLAGS`, moved after it; with a scan option before it the scan's usage error adds "bundle-check must be the first argument"; its own parser, `build_bundle_parser`): the certificate, its chain, private key and CSR checked together before installing, nothing sent, nothing secret printed (a key's PEM is kept only for haproxy.pem). A path given twice is read once (a note says so).
  - Classification (`bundle_items`): each PEM block (text around them ignored) or DER file → certificate (also PKCS#7), private key (PKCS#1, PKCS#8 / OneAsymmetricKey, SEC1; `encrypted PKCS#8` or `encrypted PEM` → "encrypted key: cannot check without a password - skipped"), CSR (subject, extensionRequest SANs, key), public key, PKCS#12 (the OpenSSL command), or not used (an `EC PARAMETERS` block, as `openssl ecparam -genkey` writes before its key, is ignored). Keys are compared by `PublicKey.ident` (`public_key_from_spki`, `parse_private_key`): RSA modulus and exponent (read from the private key), EC curve + x + parity of y (a compressed point equals the uncompressed one); an EC key file without its public key is named and skipped (no curve arithmetic), and so is an Ed25519 / Ed448 key without it — the usual PKCS#8 form, which says so; a DSA key is not compared.
  - Checks (`check_bundle` → `BundleResult`, each `OK` / `WARN` / `FAIL` / `SKIPPED`): the leaf is the end-entity certificate a key belongs to, else the first; without one, a self-signed CA certificate naming hosts in subjectAltName, whose key is in the files, or whose subject CN is a host name while it may not sign certificates (no keyUsage keyCertSign: `CertInfo.key_cert_sign` is None or False — what `openssl req -x509 -subj /CN=www.example.com` makes by default) and issued none of the other certificates is the leaf with a WARN (Firefox refuses a CA:TRUE server certificate: MOZILLA_PKIX_ERROR_CA_CERT_USED_AS_END_ENTITY) and is listed as "certificate (self-signed)", not "(root)"; CA certificates alone are a FAIL ("no server certificate in these files, only CA certificates (…)"; nothing is written, a key is SKIPPED); key ↔ certificate (a key of another certificate of the files is named); CSR ↔ certificate (plus the names it asked that the certificate lacks), or CSR ↔ key without a certificate — files with no certificate at all whose CSR was compared with a key SKIP the chain ("only the private key and the CSR were compared": a key and CSR checked before ordering pass), files with nothing compared FAIL ("no certificate in these files"); a leaf without DNS / IP subjectAltName WARNs (topic `names`: browsers ignore the subject CN; the `openssl req -addext` hint); the chain by `issued_by` (issuer / subject names and key identifiers; signatures are not verified): a leaf nothing in the files issued is a missing intermediate (FAIL, with the leaf's AIA CA Issuers URL — `CertInfo.ca_issuers` — and "unless it is a root your clients already trust"), a self-signed leaf has no chain, a chain ending at an intermediate whose issuer is absent is fine (a trusted root), a root in the files is an extra root (WARN), a file listing chain certificates out of server order a WARN (not a PKCS#7 file, whose DER SET OF holds no order: `BundleItem.pkcs7`), a certificate of another chain is left out (WARN); an expired leaf FAILs, an expired intermediate or a not-yet-valid certificate WARNs.
  - `-o DIR` (must exist) writes, only for a complete chain, `fullchain.pem` (leaf + intermediates, leaf first, no root) and `chain.pem` (the intermediates, when there are any), each replaced whole (`_replace_file`); `--write-haproxy` (needs `-o`) adds `haproxy.pem` = fullchain + the key that belongs to the leaf, owner-only on POSIX (`_write_secret`, mode 600), with a warning; without such an unencrypted key it is a FAIL. Exit codes: 0, 1 a FAIL, 2 usage (no file, unreadable, a file over 10 MB, `--write-haproxy` without `-o`, a missing directory), 3 a file not written.
  - Output (`render_bundle`): each file's items (a file name longer than `BUNDLE_FILE_COLUMN` = 32 on its own line, its items indented under it), the checks, notes, then `Written:` one file per line; file names, check texts (the AIA URL among them) and notes go through `display_text`.
- The zone hand-off files (`zone-targets.txt` with `server ip` lines and host names, and `zone-names.txt`, both with a `#` header) load as `-t` / `-n` files. A dedicated `--zone FILE` option is not built yet.
- **`--compare OLD_IP NEW_IP -n NAME`** (instead of a scan; `-t`, `--estate` and the other scan-only options are then refused, and `-t` is required otherwise: `parser.error` keeps the old message): `fetch_side()` opens one TLS connection per address with SNI = NAME (`make_client_context`, whatever certificate is served), sends one `GET --path` over that socket with `http.client` (`conn.sock` = the TLS socket; `Host: NAME[:port]`, `Accept-Encoding: identity`, `Connection: close`), reads up to `COMPARE_BODY_LIMIT` (1 MiB) and hashes it (SHA-256), reads the `<title>` (`page_title`, the charset of Content-Type; a character reference to a UTF-16 surrogate is U+FFFD, as in a browser), then one verifying handshake (`_verify_side` with `trust_context`, as the scan's trust check: `ssl.create_default_context()` without VERIFY_X509_STRICT, or `--cafile`'s CAs, the name checked; a covering certificate issued by a `--private-ca` counts as trusted, within its dates: an expired or not yet valid one is not, as a public one; `trustDetail` in the trust check's words, `expired (code 10)`). `compare_sides()` applies the web app's rules (§5.53; `cert_subject` = `cert_names_text()`, the verdict `unreachable` when neither answers) and `render_compare()` prints both answers side by side (ERROR / DIFFERS / differs marks for differences, WARNING for a problem both share — an untrusted certificate, the same one or failing alike from the same issuer (`_shared_untrust`, the web app's `sharedUntrust`: the same SHA-256; else the same verify message — Python reports one error, so a new `not_before` in the future is checked apart, and so is a new leaf sent alone where the old server sent its chain (`chain_length`, the JSON's `chainLength`, from `get_unverified_chain()`: public on Python 3.13+, on the private `_sslobj` since 3.10; unknown on 3.8 / 3.9, where only the web app's probe error tells) —, neither self-signed, and both Cloudflare Origin CA certificates (`is_origin_ca_certificate`: Cloudflare trusts its RSA and ECC CAs alike, which the web app sees as one "CloudFlare, Inc.") or the same issuer DN (`_dn_key`, as `issued_by`; an empty one never matches) with the same authority key id when both carry one), neither covering the name, both expiring soon — with a `WARNING:` line under the verdict for each, `COMPARE_SHARED`; any other untrusted certificate after an untrusted one is DIFFERS, `cert-untrusted-other`; the HSTS rules use `hsts_policy()` → `(max-age, includeSubDomains, preload, valid)`, read as the web app's `parseHsts`; neither answering is WARNING too); `--json FILE` writes `domainscope.compare/1` (`shared` included); one `-p` port, `--timeout`, `--private-ca`, `--no-color`, `-q`; `--fail-on-change` → exit 4 on `broken`, `differs` or `unreachable`, never for a problem both servers share (two identical servers are `same`). Private addresses are the point: the web app sends those here. Tests: `tests/python/test_compare_origins.py` (HTTPS servers on the same port of 127.0.0.1 and 127.0.0.2, the request on the TLS socket, same / differs / broken / closed, the same private-CA certificate on both without `--private-ca` → SAME with the shared WARNING and exit 0 under `--fail-on-change`, an internal CA's certificate then a self-signed one → DIFFERS and exit 4, the issuer rule with the origin CA and self-signed fixtures, another verify message, a new certificate not valid yet, the DN key, an empty DN, another authority key id, the RSA → ECC origin CA, HSTS as a browser reads it (joined, repeated, invalid, off, shorter, weaker), usage errors).
- Tests (`tests/python/test_ssl_origin_scan.py`; certificate kinds and ports in `test_cert_kinds_ports.py` with the `cli_*_wild` / `cli_private_ca*` / real Origin CA root fixtures; web parity in `test_inventory_targets.py`; `--estate` in `test_estate.py` — a fake fleet with every finding, the committed fixture reports, real local TLS servers with several certificates, one name on two servers with different certificates and the no-SNI default; `bundle-check` in `test_bundle_check.py` over the `bundle_*` fixtures, key material never printed; STARTTLS mail / directory / chat / database ports and `--tls-audit` in `test_starttls_audit.py`): DER parser vs `tests/fixtures/expected.json`; inventory parsing; wildcard matching; **integration**: start local TLS servers on 127.0.0.1 ephemeral ports (threads, `ssl.SSLContext.sni_callback` selecting fixture cert/key by SNI; default cert = cn_only) and assert statuses for names; `--cert` fingerprint UPDATED path.

### 7.1 CLI `cli/dns_parity.py` (Python ≥3.8, stdlib only, single file)

A script of its own rather than a mode of ssl_origin_scan.py: it shares nothing with the TLS scanner (its own zone-file reader and DNS client), it is what someone moving DNS needs without the certificate tooling, and ssl_origin_scan.py's options (targets, names, certificates, monitoring) mean nothing for it.
```
python3 dns_parity.py ZONEFILE --ns NS [NS ...] [--origin ZONE] [--port 53] [--tcp] [--timeout 3] [-w 8] [--no-extras] [--json FILE] [--csv FILE] [--show-all] [--fail-on-diff] [-q]
```
- **Zone file:** a BIND / RFC 1035 master file (`parse_zone`): `$ORIGIN` (each record keeps the one in force at its line, `Record.origin`: the relative names in its data — CNAME / NS / PTR / DNAME targets, MX and SRV hosts, a delegation's glue — follow it, as in zoneparse.js), `$TTL`, `@`, relative names, blank owners, parentheses, comments, quoted strings with escapes, TTL units, class and TTL in either order; `$INCLUDE` is not followed and `$GENERATE` not expanded (warnings); Cloudflare's `cf_tags=cf-proxied:…` / `cf-flatten-cname` comments, cli53's `AWS ALIAS` lines and `; AWS routing=` variants are read. The zone name comes from `--origin`, a leading `$ORIGIN` or the SOA owner, which then also completes the relative owners after it (a cPanel export names no `$ORIGIN`). The web app's **Download the zone (BIND)** writes a file it reads whatever the imported format was.
- **Name servers:** `--ns` host names (resolved with getaddrinfo, IPv4 first, after the zone file is read), addresses, `NAME=ADDRESS` (a host name asked at an address, before its name resolves) or `ADDRESS:PORT`; at most 8. A host name that does not resolve is UNREACHABLE in the report (a warning on stderr) and the others are asked; exit 2 only when no server can be asked. Each is asked for the zone's SOA first (`check_nameserver`: OK, REFUSED, NOT_AUTHORITATIVE, NO_ZONE, SERVFAIL, UNREACHABLE); a server that does not serve the zone is asked nothing else.
- **DNS client:** `build_query` (RD off, EDNS(0) with a 1232-byte buffer), UDP with 2 tries and TCP when the answer is truncated (or `--tcp`), the reply matched by id and question, `parse_message` with name decompression (loops and truncation are `DnsError`); A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, DNAME, MX, TXT / SPF, SRV, CAA, TLSA / SMIMEA, SSHFP, DS / CDS, NAPTR, SVCB / HTTPS (the SvcParams by key, the IP hints and the mandatory keys sorted, alpn in its order), LOC, OPENPGPKEY, URI and SOA decode to the same comparison keys as the file's values (`file_value`), and a value in RFC 3597's `\# length hex` form, of any type, is read as the rdata of an answer (`TYPEnnn` of a known type is that type), so every record set of the file is asked; a value the script cannot read is SKIPPED (`unreadable`), DNSSEC types (RRSIG, NSEC*, DNSKEY, CDNSKEY) too, aliases too, records below a delegation too (except the glue of its name servers, compared from the referral's additional section; the cut's NS from its authority section).
